title: A dominance plot asks: is one operating condition deciding the objective?
summary: The top row shows how much each condition contributes to a classical average error; the bottom row shows, per condition, whether tuning made the error fraction of nominal go down or up. Together they ask whether an average is a fair summary or whether one outlying condition is steering it.

media.alt: Two rows of three panels, one column per fuel (n-heptane, methyl butanoate, 1,3-butadiene). Top: sorted horizontal bars of each condition's share of the classical error, with a dotted uniform-share line and the largest bar labelled with a percentage. Bottom: dots on a log axis for the control and the tuned run, joined by green arrows where tuning improved a condition and red where it worsened, with a dash-dot line at 1 for nominal.

read_the_figure.question: How much of the classical average error comes from a single condition, and does a different objective spread the attention more evenly?
read_the_figure.axes: Top row, one panel per fuel: horizontal bars sorted from largest to smallest, one per condition (labelled with phi and P). x: that condition's share of the classical weighted mean relative error at the nominal mechanism, in percent. The vertical dotted line is the uniform reference, 100 divided by the number of conditions D. D is printed in each title (for example D = 12 of 17 means 12 of 17 target data sets survive). Bottom row, same conditions: x is S-hat, the relative error of that condition as a fraction of its nominal error, on a log scale; 1 means no change. Blue dot: the control run with exponent 1. Orange dot: the best tuned exponent schedule. Arrow colour: green means tuning improved this condition, red means it worsened it. The dash-dotted vertical line marks nominal, S-hat = 1.
look_at: Top row: the longest bar against the dotted line. A bar many times longer than the dotted line is one condition that carries the average. The percentage is printed beside it.
Top row: the other bars. If they are all shorter than the dotted line, the average is effectively a one-condition average.
Bottom row: the arrows. Count green against red. Note which conditions the red arrows belong to; are they the high-share ones or the low-share ones?
Bottom row: the length of the arrows. A long green arrow in a condition that had a small share shows that the tuned objective attends to conditions the classical average ignores.
Where a panel has an annotation (for example a low-temperature outlier flagged with a table number), read it: the figure itself says which condition is the outlier.
read_the_figure.proves: That the classical average is dominated by few conditions, quantitatively, and that the tuned run's per-condition outcomes are mixed rather than uniformly better. It does not prove which objective is better: dominance is the motivation for a different average, and the improvement per condition is a separate test.
if_wrong: All bars about the same length as the dotted line: no dominance, the classical average would be fine and the motivation is absent.
Many red arrows: tuning trades some conditions for others. The aggregate can still improve while individual conditions get worse.
A blue dot already below the orange dot on many rows: the control run was already better than the tuned run on those conditions.
A different D in each panel: the fuels have different numbers of surviving data sets, so their uniform reference lines are at different places.
must_check: D, the number of conditions, is printed so that the reference share 100/D can be checked.
The log axis of S-hat has a labelled reference at 1 (nominal).
Colour is not the only carrier of the improved or worsened message: the arrow direction also shows it.
Bars are sorted, which makes the dominance readable; check that the order is the same in both rows.
The shares sum to 100 percent: the visible bars should be consistent with that.

terms.meaning: A condition's contribution divided by the sum of all contributions. For an average of relative errors, a condition's share is its error over the sum of errors.
A single condition carrying a large part of the total, so that the average mostly reflects it.
The share each condition would have if all counted equally: one over D.
A condition's relative error after tuning divided by its relative error at the nominal mechanism. Below 1 is an improvement.
For positive numbers s_1..s_D, the generalized mean of exponent p. It is an ordinary average when p = 1, a geometric mean as p goes to 0, and it approaches the largest value as p grows.
The same procedure with the classical exponent (p = 1): the comparison that isolates the effect of the new objective.
A data set whose error is far larger than the others, often from a different regime (here a low-temperature one).

remember: An average hides its largest term. Plot the shares to see it.
The share is s over the sum of the s: it is the fraction of the total, not the fraction of the data.
The uniform reference is 100 / D percent.
The geometric mean (p going to 0) gives every condition equal weight in a relative-improvement sense.
A good aggregate can come with individual conditions getting worse: look for red arrows.

understand.title: Why the bars are sorted
understand.text: Sorted bars make the dominance a visual fact: the first bar is the biggest, and the staircase down shows how fast the remaining conditions fall away. The dotted line then gives a yardstick for what equal weight would look like.

understand.title: Why S-hat is on a log axis
understand.text: A halving and a doubling should be mirror images. On a log axis they are symmetric about 1, so improvements and deteriorations of the same factor have the same visual length.

understand.title: The companion bar chart
understand.text: A related figure in the project page compares the mean error of the nominal mechanism, the classical average and the tuned objective for the three fuels. The ordering is nominal worst and tuned best in every fuel, and the gap between the classical and the tuned bars is largest where one condition dominates. A single bar per fuel hides the per-condition story this plot shows, and has no uncertainty on it.

steps.title: The power mean of a set of errors
steps.note: Standard definition. Raising to p before averaging changes how much each condition counts: a large p lets the largest errors dominate the average, a small p lets all conditions count more evenly.

steps.title: p = 1 is the ordinary average
steps.note: This is the classical mean of the errors. One condition with a very large error can supply most of the total.

steps.title: Share of the classical average
steps.note: This is what each top-row bar shows, in percent. One term with a large s makes its w close to one.

steps.title: Sensitivity of a power mean to a relative improvement
steps.note: Differentiate M_p with respect to s_d and multiply by s_d. For p = 1 the pull of a condition on the objective is its share of the total, exactly the top-row bar. As p goes to 0 every condition has the same pull, 1 over D: that is the dotted line.

steps.title: The uniform reference line
steps.note: Computed from the D printed in the panel titles. The dotted lines in the three panels sit at these places.

steps.title: Ratio on a log axis
steps.note: Equal differences in ln S-hat are equal factors, so an arrow of a given length is the same factor of change wherever it sits on the axis.

worked.title: How the exponent redistributes the weight
worked.problem: Four conditions have relative errors 4.0, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 (illustrative numbers). What share does the largest carry for p = 1, p = 0.5 and p = 0.05?

solution.text: Share is the power of s over the sum of powers. For p = 1 the sum is 5.0.
For p = 0.5 the powers are 2.0, 0.71, 0.55, 0.45 with a sum of 3.70.
For p = 0.05 the shares are nearly equal.

worked.answer: 80 percent, 54 percent and 27.5 percent: lowering the exponent moves the weight from the worst condition toward equal weight, 25 percent each.

analyze.q: One bar carries almost the whole top-row panel. Which conditions get almost no attention from the classical average and what does that mean for tuning?
Red arrows appear on conditions with small shares. Is that surprising?
analyze.hint: The new objective gives those conditions more weight; a move can still trade them off.

analyze.q: Two panels have a similar top bar but different D. Are they equally dominated?
analyze.hint: Compare each bar with its own dotted line.

evaluate.q: Does the dominance plot show that the tuned objective is better, or only why a different objective was needed?
Would you remove the outlier condition from the fit? Argue both sides.
evaluate.hint: It may be a real regime the mechanism cannot reproduce, or an unreliable measurement; either way it should be reported, not silently dropped.

create: Add a third row to the figure that shows, per condition, the change in absolute and relative error with the sign, so that red arrows can be sized by their effect on the aggregate.
Design a test of how the number of surviving conditions D changes the dominance if conditions are dropped at random.

checks.q: What does the dotted line in the top row mean?
checks.answer: The share each condition would have if all counted equally: 100 divided by D percent.

checks.q: Four conditions have errors 6, 2, 1 and 1. What share does the first carry for the classical average?
A green arrow for a low-share condition and a red arrow for the top-share condition. What did the tuning do?
checks.hint: Which conditions the average attends to.
checks.answer: It traded the high-share condition for improvement elsewhere. The aggregate may still go down, but the dominant condition got worse and should be examined.

checks.q: Why is a single bar-chart of means per fuel not enough?
checks.answer: It hides the distribution across conditions, the outliers and the red arrows, and it carries no uncertainty. The dominance plot shows which conditions produced the mean.

checks.q: How would you show that the effect is not only because one condition dominates?
checks.answer: Recompute the comparison with the dominant condition left out, and plot the aggregate with and without it for both objectives.
